open-question.question: Some of the historical cases chosen for the one-off check come from milestones that predate `open_questions.xml`, where the question blocks sit inside `requirements.md` and the alternatives pass stops on the open-question tool's `Error:` line. How are those cases re-run?

The one-off check counts the change as verified when the new rules recover the missing direction in clearly more of the re-run cases than the unchanged rules, with the margin fixed before the runs. What is that margin?
The new-rules run and the baseline run of the one-off check use the same model and effort setting. Which model and effort setting do they use?
open-question.alternative: Both runs use `--model "opus"` at `--effort xhigh`. This is the setting `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` gives every `provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions` line, and it is the one used on every re-run case and control case. The verdict measures the rules under the conditions the alternatives pass actually runs in. A recovery margin found here carries straight over to the documented chains, with no reasoning needed about a different model or effort level. At a high effort level the unchanged rules may already recover many missing directions. That ceiling can shrink the gap the check has to show, so whether this setting clears the bar depends on the margin the Recovery margin value question fixes. Also, `opus` is a family alias that resolves to the latest release, so both runs must happen while the alias points at the same release.

Both runs use `--model "opus"` at `--effort max`, the highest effort Claude Code accepts. The check tests the rules at the most reasoning the host can give, above the documented pass setting. The comparison gives each rule version its best chance. If the new rules still recover clearly more missing directions at maximum effort, the gain comes from the wording and cannot be explained by extra reasoning budget. No documented chain runs the alternatives pass at `max`, so the result describes a setting nobody uses for this pass. It is also the costliest and slowest option: every case is run twice, the paired baseline and the new rules. And the ceiling effect is at its strongest here, which can leave too little gap for whatever margin its sibling question fixes.

Both runs use a lower effort than the documented pass: `--effort high` or below, on `opus` or `fable`. Every setting in that range has the same trade-off, cheaper runs that depend more on the written rules. The chosen setting is used for every re-run case and control case. With less reasoning budget, the enumerator relies more on what the procedure tells it to do. The difference between the old and new wording is then less likely to be hidden by the model finding missing directions by itself, and running twice per case costs less. The alternatives pass is never run at this setting in the documented chains. A margin found here may not hold at `xhigh`, and a verdict of "verified" could overstate the gain in real use.

The requirements fix no model or effort. The runs use whatever the executing session supplies, either host defaults with both flags omitted or a setting the runner picks when the check starts. The setting actually used is recorded next to the committed aggregate results, and both runs of each case still share it. Nothing is committed ahead of time, and nothing more has to be decided before the check can run. The pairing decision already makes the comparison fair whichever setting is used. The margin for "clearly more" is fixed before the runs, but the setting it is measured under is not. The setting could then be chosen, or rerun, after early results are seen, which weakens the fixed-in-advance principle behind the margin decision. Host defaults can also change between separate sessions, so a check spread over time may not have used one setting throughout.

open-question.question: The one-off check re-runs a small fixed sample of the refinement overrides as control cases. By what method are those control cases picked from the refinement overrides?
open-question.alternative: Pick the control cases by a random draw over every refinement override, using a seed fixed and written down before any run, with no filtering or weighting by the case's features. No one's judgment shapes which cases get in, so the new rules cannot be flattered by the choice of controls, and anyone holding the seed and the case list can reproduce the exact sample. With a small sample, chance decides the mix. The refinement overrides are heavily concentrated in one source project and mostly come from sets of three options, so the draw may miss the less common cases where a regression would show, for example a historical set that already held near-duplicates or had only two options. If a drawn case comes from a milestone that predates open_questions.xml, whether it can run at all depends on how pre-split cases end up being handled.

Split the refinement overrides into groups by features that bear on the control checks (source project, how many alternatives the historical set held, and whether the judged verdict flagged near-duplicates in it), then make a seeded random draw inside each group so every group is represented. Keeps the unbiased random choice but guarantees the sample covers the kinds of set where the new rules could plausibly lose a refined direction or add filler, rather than repeating the most common kind. It takes more setup: the grouping features have to be picked and fixed before the draw, and a small sample may not reach every group, so some groups get one case or none. How well it works depends on the sample size, which is still an open question.

Pick the control cases by a fixed rule tied to the 20 missed-direction cases: take refinement overrides from the same source milestones as those cases (with a seeded draw where there are more candidates than places), so each control shares project and period with a tested case. The controls face the same projects, rule versions, and question style as the cases the verdict rests on. A regression they show then speaks directly to whether the recovered directions came at a cost in those same settings. They can also reuse the same source checkouts. The sample carries over whatever skew the 20 strong candidates have, so it says little about refinements from milestones those cases never touch. Some of those milestones may have no refinement override at all, which leaves the rule underspecified until a fallback is chosen.

Pick the control cases by a fixed ordering rule: the most recent refinement overrides by answer-commit date, taken from newest back until the sample is full. It is fully mechanical and needs no seed. It favours cases written under the current question format and recent authoring habits, which both reduces how often a pre-split milestone turns up and makes the controls resemble the questions the rewritten rules will actually face. Recent cases cluster in time and usually in one project, so the sample covers a narrow slice of the refinement overrides. Any quirk of that recent period, such as one milestone's question style, can decide the control result.

Have a person or agent read the refinement overrides and choose the cases where the historical answer most plainly refines one listed option. Leave out borderline cases, whose verdict could just as well have been a coverage gap or a premise shift. The chosen list is fixed before any run. Each control then has a clear refined direction to check for. The "still holds that option's direction" judgment becomes crisp instead of arguable, so a failed control means a real regression rather than an ambiguous case. The choice is judgment, not a random draw, so it is open to selection bias. Clear-cut cases may be exactly the ones any rule version keeps, which makes the controls weaker at catching the subtle losses they exist to catch. The picker also has to be kept blind to how either rule version performs.

open-question.question: The one-off check re-runs a small fixed sample of the refinement overrides as control cases. How many control cases does the sample hold?
open-question.alternative: A token sample of three to five refinement overrides out of the 65 available. Each one runs under both the new rules and the unchanged baseline, since the paired baseline covers every re-run case. That adds roughly six to ten runs to the 40 needed for the 20 missed-direction cases. It is the cheapest option and matches the recorded "small fixed sample" most literally. It is still enough to catch a gross regression, where the new rules drop the direction the historical answer refined or pad the set with near-duplicates or filler, because such a failure shows up on nearly any case. It can only show that a regression exists, not how often it happens. A single failure is 20–33% of the sample, so one unusual case can swing the result. If failed controls turn out to affect the verdict (a sibling question), that verdict would rest on one or two cases. If the sample has to be stratified by some property (another sibling question), there may be fewer slots than strata.

A moderate sample of eight to ten refinement overrides, about half the size of the 20-case missed-direction set. Each case is run under both rule versions, which adds roughly 16–20 runs. It is big enough for a rough failure rate, where one failed control is about 10% rather than a third of the sample. It leaves room to spread the cases across source projects or question types, and it still stays clearly "small" next to the pool of 65. It raises the check's run count by about 40–50% and does the same for the controls' judging load. The extra cases buy little if a failed control ends up only noted rather than affecting the verdict. The judging cost also depends on who makes the two control judgments (a sibling question), which is heavier if a person rather than the blind judge agent reviews every set.

A sample of 20 refinement overrides, the same size as the missed-direction set, so the check has equal numbers of regression cases and recovery cases. Control failures and recovered directions can be reported as rates over the same number of cases in the aggregate results. Any regression the rewrite causes would then be measured with the same precision as the improvement it is meant to deliver. It doubles the check's runs and judging to about 80 runs across both rule versions. At nearly a third of the 65 refinement overrides, it stretches what the recorded decision calls a "small" sample. The eligible pool may also be smaller than 65 if pre-split cases can't be re-run as they are (a sibling question), which would make 20 cases harder to fill without letting the pool shape the selection.

open-question.question: For each control case the one-off check tests that the re-run set still holds the refined option's direction and has no near-duplicate or filler options. Who makes those two judgments: the blind judge agent that decides the missed-direction cases, or someone else?
open-question.alternative: The blind judge agent that decides the missed-direction cases also makes both control judgments. For each control case it receives an extra brief made of the historical answer, the listed option that answer refined, and the re-run set. It is not told which rule version produced the set. Every verdict the check produces comes from one judge under one blindness rule. This includes the control verdicts on the baseline sets from the paired single baseline. The user still receives only verdicts, and the milestone builds and calibrates only one judging setup. The recorded decision limits this judge's inputs to the historical answer, the recorded missing direction and the re-run set. Control cases have no missing direction, so that input contract has to be widened. Deciding whether an option is filler also takes project context the judge is deliberately not given, so its near-duplicate and filler verdicts may be shallow or inconsistent. How much that matters depends on how the sibling question on a control failure's effect settles.

A second judge agent, with its own context and blind to rule version, makes both control judgments. It gets its own brief (the historical answer, the refined option and the re-run set), and the missed-direction judge's decided inputs stay as they are. The missed-direction judge is used exactly as decided, with no changes. Blindness still covers the controls. The control brief can be written for its own two questions: whether the direction is still held, and whether any option is a near-duplicate or filler. The milestone has to write and run a second judging setup. The two judges may apply different standards, so the control and missed-direction verdicts can't be compared directly. The filler judgment still has no project grounding.

The user reads each control case's re-run set and makes both judgments by hand. Only the missed-direction cases go to the blind judge agent. Near-duplicate and filler are subjective calls. The person with the most context on the historical projects makes them, with no judge brief to design or calibrate. The user's own sense of a padded set is the standard the rewrite is meant to meet. The user usually knows which rule version is being tested, and may also know which set came from which run, so the control verdicts are not blind. That breaks the pattern the missed-direction decision set. It also adds manual reading work that grows with the sample, so its cost depends on how the sibling question on control sample size settles.

The two judgments go to different judges. The blind judge agent decides whether the refined option's direction is still held, which is the same kind of containment judgment it already makes for missed directions. The user decides whether any option is a near-duplicate or filler. Each judgment goes to the judge best suited to it. Direction containment stays blind and matches the missed-direction verdicts. The subjective filler call goes to the person who can tell padding from a real option. It combines the costs of both routes: the judge's inputs still have to be widened for control cases, and the user still has non-blind reading work for every control set. Each control case's result also depends on two judges.

The session running the one-off check, which clones each case, runs the pass and reads the sets, makes both control judgments inline as it reads each set. No separate judge is involved. This is the cheapest option. It needs no extra dispatch, no extra brief and no user effort, and the judgment is made at the moment the set is already in context. That session wrote the rewrite and knows which rule version produced each set. Its verdicts are the least independent of all the options, which is the bias the blind-judge decision was made to avoid for the missed-direction cases.

open-question.question: The one-off check's verdict is defined only by how many missing directions the new rules recover compared with the baseline. What effect does a failed control case (a lost direction, or a near-duplicate or filler option) have on whether the change counts as verified?
open-question.alternative: Control failures gate the verdict with zero tolerance. The change counts as verified only if the recovery margin is met and every control case passes both of its tests: the refined option's direction is kept, and the set has no near-duplicate or filler option. This is an absolute bar on the new-rules sets alone, and any control failure counts as falling short, which starts the single revise-and-re-run round. It gives the strongest guard against the main risk of an axes-first rewrite with no count guideline, which is a set that finds new directions by drifting away from directions users actually took or by growing filler. It also needs no extra number fixed before the runs. A single noisy judgment on one case can overturn a clear recovery gain and use up the only revision round. How fragile this is depends on how many control cases the sample holds and who judges them, both owned by sibling questions.

Control failures gate the verdict above a tolerance that is fixed before the runs. That tolerance is a count or share of control cases allowed to fail, with both failure kinds counted together. The bar is absolute on the new-rules sets alone. Exceeding the tolerance counts as falling short and starts the single revise-and-re-run round, and failures within it are reported in the aggregate results. Controls still decide the outcome, but one borderline judgment cannot sink the whole check. This matches how the recovery margin is fixed in advance. It adds a second number to choose before the runs, with nothing in the benchmark to set it by. On a small sample, any tolerance above zero is close to either a veto or no gate at all. What it means depends on the control sample size, which a sibling question owns.

Control failures gate the verdict relative to the paired baseline. The control tests are also judged on the unchanged-rules set for each control case, and the change counts as verified only if the new rules fail no more control cases than the baseline does, on both failure kinds together. Failing that comparison counts as falling short and starts the single revise-and-re-run round. It uses the same paired-comparison logic as the recovery verdict and the baseline runs that are already required. That separates real regressions caused by the rewrite from judging noise and from flaws the historical sets already had. It doubles the control judgments. It also lets the new rules keep baseline-level near-duplicates and filler (13 historical sets already had near-duplicates), even though the milestone's new distinctness rule is meant to remove them.

The verdict depends on the failure kind. A control case that loses the refined option's direction gates the verdict with zero tolerance and starts the single revise-and-re-run round. A near-duplicate or filler option is reported in the aggregate results and does not affect whether the change counts as verified. The hard gate covers the more serious failure, a pick that users actually made becoming impossible. The softer judgment of whether an option is filler is kept out of the pass/fail outcome. Growth in the set, the risk that removing the count guideline most directly invites, could still pass as verified. The distinctness rule this milestone adds would then have no enforced check.

Control failures do not affect the verdict. The verdict stays defined only by the recovery margin over the baseline, and control results of both kinds are recorded next to it in the aggregate results as advisory findings, which never start the revise-and-re-run round. The verdict stays exactly as the recorded decision defines it, and nothing new has to be fixed before the runs. Noise from a small control sample cannot overturn a clear recovery result. The change could count as verified while it loses directions users chose or pads sets with filler. That makes the control cases decoration rather than a check, and leaves any regression they reveal with no required response.

open-question.question: Only aggregate results of the one-off check may be committed, and the new `CLAUDE.md` invariant carries no measurement figures. In which committed file are the check's aggregate results recorded?
open-question.alternative: The aggregate results go in the `**Verified:**` bullets of the check's task entry in the milestone's `TASKS_DONE.md`. That file already holds each completed task's acceptance bar and evidence, so the results stay inside the milestone's own records. `docs/` and `requirements.md` stay as they are. It needs no new file and no new convention. `complete-procedure.md` already writes the evidence for a finished task into `**Verified:**` bullets, so recording the recovered-direction counts, the baseline counts, the margin, and the control outcomes there fits the pipeline exactly. The milestone directory also keeps its fixed set of four files. The results sit in the milestone's task record, which is mainly read by later runs of that milestone's own completion. Anyone checking design claim 4 or the new `CLAUDE.md` invariant would have to know which milestone and which task to open. Whether the results end up split across several task entries also depends on how `derive-tasks` breaks up the check.

The aggregate results go in the milestone's `requirements.md`, as a verification-outcome entry under `## Decisions` next to the verification decisions it measures. `TASKS_DONE.md` points to that entry and does not repeat the figures. The result sits right beside the bar, the baseline design, and the fallback rule it is judged against, which include "records the aggregate shortfall". A reader of the requirements sees both the rule and whether it passed in one place. `## Decisions` holds choices, not measurements. A result entry would mix outcomes into a section that the answer core folds decisions into and that `capture-milestone-principle-updates` and review passes read as decisions. It is also written after the requirements have converged, which is not how that file is normally used.

The aggregate results go in this milestone's entry under `## Milestone History` in `milestones/README.md`, written by `finish-current-milestone` as one or two summary bullets. No other committed file carries the figures. The finish step writes this summary anyway, and it is the project-wide record a new session reads first. The outcome becomes visible across milestones with no extra file and no extra step. History bullets are short accomplishment lines written at finish time. Several counts plus a baseline comparison and control outcomes would crowd them. The figures also would not exist in any committed place until the milestone finishes, so a revise-and-re-run round in between leaves no committed record.

The aggregate results go in `docs/design-claims.md` under claim 4, as a short evidence statement next to its unchanged Metric line. That records a first measured result for the claim about alternative quality. The result sits in the public document that makes the claim it supports. That makes it the most useful place for outside readers and for the grant and benchmark goals, and it turns a claim the page says no suite tests into one with recorded evidence. It changes the structure of a page whose claims all follow a fixed Design/Metric shape, and it goes beyond the recorded documentation decision, which rewrites only claim 4's Design and keeps its Metric line. A one-off, single-model result from a small sample may also read as a stronger or more lasting guarantee than it is.

The aggregate results go in a new committed file of their own outside the milestone directory, for example a verification-results page under `docs/`. That page holds the counts, the margin, the baseline comparison, and the control outcomes, and other records link to it. There is room for the full aggregate picture without crowding any existing format. The file could also later hold the results of the committed benchmark harness that the uncommitted `temp/` idea document proposes. It adds a new committed document and a new convention for a one-off check. That page then has to be listed in `CLAUDE.md`'s repository layout and kept current. It also raises a greater risk that details from the private benchmark leak past "aggregate results and generic pattern descriptions" as the page grows.

The aggregate results stay only in the uncommitted `temp/` benchmark material and are reported to the user in the session. No committed file records them, and the committed artifacts state the rules without any evidence. There is no chance at all that anything from the benchmark data or the private projects reaches a committed artifact. No committed format has to change to hold measurements. The recorded decisions expect a committed outcome ("records the aggregate shortfall", "counts as verified"), so none of this milestone's evidence would survive in git. That goes against the principle that the repository is the memory, and a later reader could not tell whether the rewrite was ever verified.

open-question.question: The one-axis authoring rule is verified by running `review-milestone-requirements` against a synthetic fixture with one independent pair and one coupled pair of axes. What does the milestone do when that run does not author the questions as expected?
